stories.title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
stories.summary: The post Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Experiments with the rule of law around the world are creating the kind of resiliency we need in our era of uncertainty.

MUNICH — Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty.

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

Our societies have long considered the law a slow and steady force, “the essential foundation of stability and order” in the words of J. William Fulbright. To that end, law is backward-looking — “the government of the living by the dead,” according to Oliver Wendell Holmes. The lawmaking process in republics and democracies is age-old: observe a problem, study its particularities, debate solutions and then carve out a rule that will endure for years or decades.

But what happens when the future arrives faster than your regional regulator or local parliament can make a rule?

The emerging answer is experimental law or, in Germany, where Munich is a hotbed, Experimentierklauseln . “Experimental clauses” refer to sections and parts of laws that are made flexible, often for set time periods, to allow for real-time adaptation or alteration in response to changing threats, climate or technology.

The shift toward such experimentation has begun, albeit slowly, in only certain areas of the law. Contract law and administrative law, especially where they touch on technology or other advanced sectors of the economy, are becoming more fluid.

Contracts, once used to protect against all contingencies, are now written more openly — explicitly anticipating new knowledge and adjustments. Among startups and innovation-oriented companies, written agreements are less likely to specify payments for specific work at specific times and more likely to establish processes for collaboration and shared decision-making.

For example, start-ups use Agile contracts with vendors that, instead of pledging a final digital product at a price, set parameters of a creative process involving a test phase, iterative feedback loops and product benchmarks. Biotech startups rely on a “relational contract” with manufacturers to create a collaboration framework that includes regular meetings, shared lab notes and a commitment to use best efforts to scale a prototype.

Meanwhile, smart contracts have become commonplace in supply chains to allow for real-time changes in inventory levels. Union contracts in digital workplaces often incorporate adaptive provisions — “continuous bargaining” in 21st-century labor parlance — with guidelines for how workers participate across the lifecycles of systems and products.

Modern tech procurement uses what’s called “Dynamic Service Level Agreements” that feature automatic updates, scalable license adjustments, and continuous remote monitoring and interventions by seller and buyer. “Data Processing Agreements” within cloud contracts dynamically adjust data handling and security protocols as privacy regulations and digital risks shift. In some cases, AI agents have written contracts in code rather than in English. Put simply, some contracts now write themselves.

Similarly, regulatory agencies and public administrations have moved away from the time-consuming traditional rulemaking process, since rules quickly become outdated in a world so strange and fast-changing. Instead, agencies and administrative judges, particularly in advanced economies, are more likely to offer “guidance” — advisories, memos, letters or protocols that are regularly tweaked or edited in response to updated knowledge and changing circumstances.

These shifts point toward an emerging and quite radical recognition, especially in law, that extreme uncertainty is not a problem to be solved, but a reality and even an ally. The fact that the future is too hard for anyone to know is leveling. The regulator, the regulated and the everyday person all know the same thing: almost nothing.

The act of lawmaking then becomes a great collaboration between governments and experts and firms and workers and the regular people most affected. And that collaboration is a search, never-ending, for improvements and innovations and solutions.

Such collaboration turns lawmaking as we know it on its head. Implementation is required first to understand what the policy should be. In this new paradigm, resilience is grounded in fragility. Resilience does not come from buffering organizations against known risks, but by designing them to show quickly when they are broken, so they can be reconfigured. It is a kind of deliberately induced and carefully controlled institutional fragility. Strain is immediately apparent, triggering investigation and countermeasures well before it ramifies into catastrophe.

“Experimental clauses allow for real-time adaptation in response to changing threats, climate or technology.”

Climate Changes The Law

The stakes of achieving this new, more open mentality are expressed perhaps most clearly in our response to global warming. In the 2022 book, “Fixing the Climate: Strategies for an Uncertain World,” Columbia Law School’s Charles F. Sabel and UC San Diego’s David G. Victor argue that decades of top-down global climate diplomacy — from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement — have failed because they rely on inflexible global treaties.

Treaties are among the oldest forms of law. But climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly. And they don’t reflect the reality that climate change impacts — and opportunities to mitigate and adapt to climate change — are very different depending on location and context. (Sea level rise is not an issue in Mongolia; glacial melting does not plague Phoenix). The only viable way to make law and government is thus through relentless, highly structured and broadly collaborative local experimentation. This model, they noted, is neither “top down” nor “bottom up” but both at the same time.

“Our central aim is to reorient our current climate change regime away from failed efforts based on ex ante global consensus, and toward a system anchored in local and sectoral experimentalism and learning,” they wrote .

This local experimentalist mindset is emerging especially in the metro regions of countries that have advanced economies and histories of collaborative lawmaking and regulation.

Two places that best fit that description are Singapore, which was built on deep cooperation between government technocrats and industry, and Germany’s bigger cities.

Experimental law first emerged in West Germany during the 1950s as a pragmatic mechanism for the Länder, or states, to exploit their autonomy under the 1949 Basic Law. Faced with ideological divisions and a lack of national precedent for building a post-authoritarian society, municipal and state agencies used “trial clauses” to break legacy rules on welfare, housing and local administrative reorganizations without setting precedents or locking local governments into long-term mandates. The first official Experimentierklauseln allowed public schools to violate rigid curricular and education standards and test pedagogies, grading systems and models of comprehensive schools.

Experimental clauses fell out of fashion in the late 20th century but were revived for new challenges in the 21st century. In 2008, the Upper Saxony town of Bohmte, Germany , used an experimental clause to do something otherwise illegal: eradicate traffic lanes, street lines, traffic lights and stop signs to combat chronic speeding, utilizing a Dutch idea called shared space .

Over the last decade, climate change and advances in technology and transportation inspired so much local experimentalism that the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action issued an official “Guide for Formulating Experimentation Clauses” in 2024. The guide runs 34 pages but contains three main rules: All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.

Ask the federal ministry staff for a signature example, and you’ll hear about a Hamburg hospital that couldn’t get cancer tissue samples to a laboratory in time because of city traffic. The hospital wanted to use a drone instead, but German aviation regulations strictly forbid drones from flying “beyond the visual line of sight” of their operators over settled urban areas.

Instead of waiting years for federal airspace reform, Hamburg relied on experimental clauses to deviate from the federal Air Traffic Act for 18 months. During that time, the city-state established the U-Space Sandbox, a 30-square-kilometer experimental airspace over the Port of Hamburg.

Officials of the local and national governments worked with two German companies, Droniq and DFS Deutsche Flugsicheruntegration, to test the integration of drones with manned aviation. The experimentation eventually produced guidance and rules for a drone air traffic system, which are being incorporated into drafts of Germany’s federal U-Space Act.

“Climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly.”

Living With Experimental Law

In Munich, I spent an evening inside one product of experimental law: an unusual new house at Goerzerstrasse 128, in the southeast neighborhood of Giesing. Munich, like so many cities, suffers from high housing prices and rents. The city held a competition for alternative solutions, and a self-organized housing syndicate won. It then used experimental clauses to deviate from strict German building codes.

The building was constructed with simple wood and cheap corrugated iron — what residents call “Favela-style” — and operates internally as a massive “shed flat.” The design is energy-efficient, and the roof captures rainwater in an underground cistern and feeds it directly back into the local groundwater table to combat drought. Read Noema in print.

The cost exceeded 3 million euros, drawn from public subsidies and private loans. But that’s cheap, given its scale. For now, 14 people — 13 adults and a six-year-old — share the open architecture, with frequent visitors. (A rock band was just leaving as I arrived.) The building is designed so it could be divided into at least nine separate apartments. While one-bedroom apartments in Munich rent for 1,700 euros a month, rent at Gorzer 128 is about 460 euros per person.

Gorzer 128 and other experiments helped inspire a national experimental clause called “Construction Turbo” (Section 246e of the German Federal Building Code), which allows municipalities to bypass existing planning standards until the end of 2030. The only unhappiness has come from neighbors who don’t like the building’s appearance (a jumble of metal and wood, quite different than the single-family craftsman homes on the street) and have been slow to engage with residents. Experimental law offers no cure for NIMBYism, at least not yet.

Beyond Gorzer 128, Munich’s experimental laws are most associated with efforts to transform streetscapes. A signal success is on the Kolumbusstraße, which a few years ago was a standard urban artery, lined with 120 concrete parking slots and choked with traffic.

Oliver May-Beckmann, who leads the MCube mobility cluster at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), says his group used an experimental clause to close the street to traffic for six months to create a Sommerstraße (Summer Street). Some drivers and residents complained to local officials. But because the project was a temporary and science-driven Reallabor , or real-world laboratory, politicians could push responsibility onto May-Beckmann and the scientists. “They’d say, ‘It’s just an experiment, let’s wait for the data,” he recalls.

For half a year , Kolumbusstraße became a green space where children could play, residents could spend time and new forms of mobility were tested. The transformation was deliberately temporary, and after six months, the street returned to its previous state. But the evaluation produced a striking result: 66% of residents supported making the changes permanent. Whether and how to turn the experiment into a lasting transformation is now a decision for the City of Munich.

MCube also used an experimental clause to test a car-sharing strategy in Nymphenburg, an affluent neighborhood that houses Munich’s botanical garden. For 20 years, Germany’s car industry — BMW, Mercedes, Sixt — had been testing different forms of free-floating vehicle-sharing to try to cut emissions, but it just put more cars on the street because people used shared vehicles on top of their own. In MCube’s test, 10 local families gave up their private cars for 18 months, and MCube bought five electric cars, plugged into charging stations in an underground garage, for the families to share. It was a closed group — the sharing was just between the 10 households, and you knew who had the car before you.

The families communicated with each other and shared the cars well. MCube also discovered that when people know a car is always nearby, they were willing to pay significantly more in regular payments for access than they would pay with one-off models. MCube is now working with both BMW and Sixt, the Bavaria-based rental car company, to spread the model around Germany. The experimental clause is still in effect and is being used to test alternative car-sharing models in three other Munich neighborhoods.

Experimental clauses offer flexibility but demand deep collaboration with business, governments and everyday people, May-Beckmann says. Take MINGA , a new project that plans to put autonomous buses on Munich’s streets this fall. (Minga is both the name for Munich in the Bavarian dialect and an acronym for Münchens Automatisierter Integrations-Nahverkehr mit Gesellschaftlicher Akzeptanz, or “Munich Automated Public Transport with Ridepooling, Solo Bus and Bus Platoons.”

The project, which uses driverless vehicles without a set schedule or route, is enabled by experimental clauses derived from 2021 amendments to Section 1i of the German Road Traffic Act. The German government is providing 13 million euros in funds. MAN, a German commercial vehicle manufacturer, built the buses. Technical University of Munich scientists have worked on the software, the public transport administration is preparing to run the buses, and the city of Munich plans to operate the service for two years under experimental clauses and then evaluate it. Finally, it requires people to sign up, primarily to bridge the “first-mile/last-mile” gap of getting people to public transit hubs.

Experimental clauses, at their best, create space and permission for systems integration. That’s nearly impossible in conventional governance, where decisions are made sequentially, and services and programs are added one by one.

“Our goal is transferring knowledge into prototypes and bringing those into real life,” says May-Beckmann. “It’s crucial in Europe that mobility innovation isn’t just about a new car; it’s about a system. How do you integrate autonomous driving, city development, climate change and energy? We get funding to have industry and public administration work for us as a system.”

“All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.”

Experiments In Sunshine & Medicine

The desire to experiment with law is not exclusively German. Barcelona placed the 22@ Innovation District under experimental law to test drones. In the UK, Bethesda and other Welsh cities have employed experimental clauses for “ Sunshine Tariffs ” to encourage renewable energy use. South Korea carved out an experimental exception in its transportation laws to install a hydrogen-powered mobility system in Gyeongsangbuk-do. In Japan, the experimental mantle is carried by the “Future Design” movement, where citizens in towns like Yahaba wear differently colored robes to design infrastructure plans for future generations.

If democracy doesn’t have to be part of the legal equation, then East Asia might be the world’s leader. Singapore, the world leader in temporary regulations, has built a financial powerhouse by permitting banking and fintech experiments for decades. More recently, it has been applying experimentalism to medicine. An ongoing Health Sciences Authority experiment allows low- to medium-risk AI medical software to be used in public hospitals before formal registration. If the AI performs well for 12 months under clinician oversight, it can get an accelerated pathway to permanent approval.

More broadly, China and India have survived and prospered during rapid transitions by making experimentation a foundational principle of governance, often at the municipal or provincial levels.

In his 2024 book “Experimentalist Constitutions,” Peking University legal scholar Yueduan Wang details the Chinese government’s use of “experimental zones” to deviate from national law. In several areas, including green energy and mobility, municipalities have explicit legislative permission to try things. For example, the Shenzhen People’s Congress passed the 2025-2026 “Decision on Amending the Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Intelligent Connected Vehicles,” which allows fully driverless commercial taxis to bypass national safety standards.

India has embedded what it calls “regulatory sandbox” clauses directly into legislative updates. The Telecommunication Act of 2023 explicitly created a live testing environment that exempts companies from standard licensing fees to test 6G internet. Gujarat, where Narendra Modi served as chief before becoming national prime minister, is an epicenter of experimentation. It houses India’s first operational “smart city,” Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, to test flexible financial regulations. Many of its startups use an “interoperable sandbox” to temporarily bypass rules on corporate governance, liquidity, capital minimums, reporting timelines and marketing as they test hybrid fintech products.

Experimental Enough For AI?

Despite successes in fintech, mobility and housing, it is unclear whether experimental law will be fast or flexible enough for the ethereal, borderless realm of artificial intelligence.

In Germany, companies working with AI complain that experimental law remained too slow and earthbound to keep up. Ironically, they blame the European Union’s attempts to “lead” on experimental law and AI for the failure.

In 2024, the EU embraced experimental law with its landmark AI Act. Article 57 of the AI Act included an explicit mandate for experimental law — every member state was required to establish at least one national “AI regulatory sandbox” by August 2026. But the mandate made the program politically divisive within several countries. In a dozen member states, including Germany and France, governments couldn’t even agree on which national agency or authority would establish their sandbox. The EU acknowledged the dysfunction this summer, pushing the deadline for a national AI mandate back a year to August 2027, via the AI Omnibus .

Few in Europe’s AI policymaking community expect to meet that deadline. The trouble goes beyond the EU’s slow bureaucracy. It’s hard to employ experimental law when you’re terrified of real impacts and results. Notably, the AI Act doesn’t require experimental deployment of AI regulation in the real world. As a result, those nations that are moving toward an AI regulatory sandbox are limiting experiments to theoretical exercises or purely legal assessments. But it’s impossible to create experimental laws for AI in the real world if you won’t experiment with AI in the real world.

In Munich, Till Klein, head of regulation at the non-profit “appliedAI Institute for Europe,” says that regulatory sandboxes that do exist for AI simply have too many restrictions to be useful. “Policymakers act like sandboxes will fix all the new rules,” says Klein. “But a sandbox is more like a sniper rifle than a shotgun; your experiment has to be precise for it to be meaningful.”

His colleague Demian Niemeyer, a lawyer and senior AI regulatory expert at appliedAI, sees the choke point as cultural. “People trained in law here are trained in a ‘Bismarck mindset,’” he says. “They are incredibly risk-averse. If you want to make something better and understand risks, you need a trial-and-error mindset.”

The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation. Another fear also hamstrings experimental law: fear of regulatory capture.

That’s understandable, since effective experimental law requires regulators to collaborate closely with companies and stakeholders. Experimental law challenges the conception of regulation and law as walls between the watcher and the watched.

“The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation.”

In 2024 and 2025, fear of capture stirred controversy and delayed the drafting of Germany’s federal Reallabore-Gesetz (Regulatory Sandboxes) Act, an attempt to go beyond experimental clauses on particular subjects and create a broader framework for experimental law.

The Social Democrats, left-wing groups and some scholars argue that broad authorization of experimental clauses risks turning into backdoor-lobbying channels for Big Tech and powerful corporations seeking exemptions from labor, safety and privacy laws. Most of the objections were AI-focused.

In response, the proposed law’s backers incorporated regulatorisches Lernen (regulatory learning) as a sandbox objective. When a project is approved under an experimental clause, the outcomes cannot remain hidden. The law requires continuous evaluation of the testing, and the resulting insights must be reported transparently. There are limited exclusions for genuine intellectual property.

The law also seeks to avoid narrow regulatory discussions between a company and a government agency via a “Regulatory Sandboxes Innovation Portal.” The portal is supposed to facilitate broad co-creation of law by connecting stakeholders from business, academia, public administration and civil society.

The legislation, renamed the Bundeserprobungsgesetz (Federal Proving Act), passed the Bundestag in late June. A second legislative body, the Bundesrat, would formally enact it as law in September. At the Munich Urban Colab, the immediate reaction was uncertainty. People would have to experiment with the new law and see.

Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.

A day after his address to the Commons , the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.

After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.

But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.

“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.

In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

after newsletter promotion

Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.

However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.

“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.

The chancellor outlined ‘the biggest wave of devolution in a generation’ – but large swathes of the country are excluded

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England.

Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control.

This was the message from John Healey’s first budget , which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.

He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy.

It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.”

However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.

Manchester, the West Midlands and Liverpool City region head a list of 14 areas already governed by a mayor.

Healey said the 14 were on course to get enhanced deals, while ministers were in the final stages of signing 10 more agreements, creating MSAs for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.

Last month, Essex county council leaders agreed to adopt an MSA to secure about £1.2bn of funding over 10 years. Cornwall’s leaders, who secured a special devo deal under the previous Tory government, were at No 10 North last week – the hub of devolution discussions – hammering out an enhanced set of powers matched by extra money.

Yet there is concern that while these areas might come on board before next year, many others will be left out.

Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit, a thinktank, said: “A rewired state needs every tier of government to play its part, and it needs every tier of government to be financially resilient.”

In his view, those areas without a mayor, or without a special devo deal like Cornwall, will begin to fall behind the rest, exacerbating regional inequality.

Next month, No 10 is due to publish the much-anticipated Rewiring the State delivery plan, which Burnham has said will contain the thrust of what he wants to achieve as prime minister.

Carr-West said the holes in Healey’s speech will need to be filled in by Burnham if there is to be some clarity about the way forward. “Today’s budget statement puts more, rather than less, pressure on that document,” he said.

One of the major barriers to progress is likely to be the stalled reorganisation of local government in England, which was due to convert county and district councils into a web of unitary authorities. Angela Rayner, the secretary of state for housing, local government and communities, suspended the plan in September.

Unitary authorities will carry out all the roles previously divided between counties and districts, from providing social services and education to overseeing parking and local business licences.

Several county councils have used judicial reviews to challenge the plans, forcing Rayner to rethink.

Kent is an example of an authority that is a long way from having an MSA, after the Reform UK-run county council objected to a government plan for a split into four unitaries. It has gone to court saying Kent should remain as a single entity, much like Cornwall.

Vince Maple, head of Medway council in Kent, accepts the dispute is a barrier to a deal at the moment, but says it was clear from Healey’s speech that local government reorganisation (LGR) will go ahead in some form and devo deals will follow.

“Government has made itself clear that LGR is going ahead. Most people accept it will happen,” he said.

Maple also heads the Key Cities Group of second-tier urban areas, which includes Gloucester, Sunderland and Salford. He said the expansion of MSAs to include a further 10 areas meant the government was getting closer to its “every postcode” target.

“Our members will be part of the conversation now in a way that they weren’t 24 hours ago,” he said.

There is also scepticism that the economic growth Burnham hopes to achieve from devolution may be slow to materialise.

In a judgment on the budget, the consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.”

Burnham will hope that rearranging the structure of local government will be enough at the next election to convince voters that change is beneficial, even if he cannot show a boost to economic growth.

OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 live – latest updates

British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said.

As John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued its report showing a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances, despite the measures taken by the chancellor .

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help with soaring energy costs, the watchdog said household disposable incomes after taking account of inflation would fall by 0.6% next year. The downgrade - compared with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes that the OBR was forecasting in March – was driven mainly by higher energy costs.

While forecasting a modest recovery from next year, the OBR warned that families were facing among the weakest decades for growth in real household disposable income on records dating back to the 1960s.

Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said disposable incomes in 2029, after taking account of inflation, were on track to be only 1% higher than in 2019 – before the onset of the Covid pandemic.

“It’s a pretty grim picture”, David Miles of the OBR said.

“If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said.

“That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.”

As the impact from Donald Trump’s war hits British households, businesses and the government finances, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for countries worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule , which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.

As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

after newsletter promotion

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills .

However, with the fallout from the war steadily mounting, the OBR warned that Britain’s resilience to the conflict that had been recorded so far this year would begin to fizzle out.

While it upgrades its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, it slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.

“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

Published 29 October 2026, 12:50 GMT

People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election Published 4 hours ago

What we now know about the UK economy in four charts Published 19 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published Just now

In response the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains made in the first five years.

Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.

The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.

Lost decade

Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.

Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.

However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.

While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.

The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.

"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," added the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).

"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."

'Fragile' finances

IFS director Helen Miller said there would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament.

"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.

"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.

Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.

Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.

He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.

Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" of the amount of buffer the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

Payments to 20m homes part of package to cut energy bills and ease cost of living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks.

In his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said, announcing the payment.

The relief on bills comes at a cost to big banks via the banking surcharge rise, and to savers and landlords, who were hit with an unexpected tax rise.

Healey said his budget would shape Britain’s future on defence, energy, welfare and entrepreneurship. “This Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it.”

The chancellor also extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July, and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would help businesses as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.

He blamed the war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Healey nevertheless promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30, but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March. He said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”

The chancellor said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks and the unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.

after newsletter promotion

He is doubling the additional levy the banks pay on their profits to 6% from the current 3% for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that many industry figures had expected.

Healey lavished praise on the sector as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

There was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness.

There will be no easing of fiscal drag, however, despite Andy Burnham previously expressing concern at the rate at which households were being pulled into higher rates of income tax.

Forecasts show that the freeze on tax thresholds will drag an extra 6.7m people into paying income tax and push 5.4m more into the higher rate band by 2031–32. The minimum wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, an increase of £910 to the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker.

Pensions will also rise thanks to the triple lock, but with new tax relief to keep pensioners from paying income tax as the state pension rises above the personal allowance for the first time. About 500,000 pensioners are to benefit.

Healey also announced sweeping new powers for regions, pledging all mayors would be given a share of income tax revenue from 2028. He said he intended that local and regional government would retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade.

He said the devolution package would be “new powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics”.

Burnham insists letter telling ministers not to argue for specific UK-EU renegotiation outcomes doesn't mean they're gagged

Andy Burnham has rejected claims that he has stopped ministers speaking out about his plans for a closer relationship with Europe.

As mentioned earlier (see 12.14pm ), Burnham wrote to ministers yesterday saying he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process” as he opens a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU. At GB News, this has been written up under the headline: “Andy Burnham gags Cabinet on rejoin EU plot”.

Asked if he was preventing ministers from speaking out in his pooled interview with broadcasters today, Burnham replied:

double quotation mark Not in the slightest. I have been working with the cabinet on the approach that we’re taking to Europe, and we have a clear approach now as we go into the next UK-EU summit, which is three weeks away.

For the record, this is what Burnham said in the letter sent to cabinet ministers yesterday.

double quotation mark I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain. It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.

Burnham said that at the UK-EU summit on 20 November he wanted to lock in deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But he said he would also set out the next steps for considering the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU. He went on:

double quotation mark Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality. I am also clear that any fundamental change to the direction of the relationship would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament.

Burnham said there was an “agreed mandate” in government for the summit. He went on:

double quotation mark In the period beyond the summit, government policy will be to explore options for the long-term relationship with the EU for consideration in the next parliament. At the end of this process, we will set out to the country the respective merits and drawbacks of the various options. It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period. It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.

Healey says he does not accept joining EU single market would automatically be good for growth

John Healey did not just sound sceptical about rejoining the single market, or the EU proper, in his GB News interview. (See 12.14pm .) In an interview with LBC, he said that he did not accept the growth would automatically be better if the UK were in the single market.

Asked by the presenter, Nick Ferrari , if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU, or the single market, Healey replied:

double quotation mark Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient. It’s confounded the forecasters.

When it was put to him that being in the single market could boost GDP by 4-5%, Healey said:

double quotation mark Well, that’s part of a bigger conversation that the prime minister wants the country to have because he recognises - and everybody, many other people do – that our Brexit deal was not a good one. It’s not been good for Britain over the last decade. But my job now is to make sure, when you’re talking about growth, is to try and reinforce that resilience in the British economy.

Most economists believe being in the single market would boost UK growth significantly. But it would also involve aligning with EU regulations and allowing free movement, which Brexiters view as politically unacceptable.

It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.

Burnham says he's confident economy will go 'from strength to strength'

Andy Burnham has claimed that the British economy is going “from strength to strength”.

Economists have argued that the documents published alongside the budget suggest this parliament will be dire for living standards. (See 10.21am .) But, asked about the country’s economic prospects when speaking to reporters on a visit in Derby, Burnham said:

double quotation mark The British economy is defying the expectations of forecasters, so this year we will grow more strongly. The growth forecast has been upgraded. The IMF [International Monetary Fund] said last week we’re the standout nation for deficit reduction, so it remains difficult because the world is difficult and the situation in the Middle East has an impact. But I think people should look at what the chancellor said yesterday, see a country that has got a platform of stability in the economy. We’re beginning to defy those expectations, and I’m confident that we will go from strength to strength from here.

Burnham claims government working 'flat out' to cut welfare spending

Andy Burnham has said the government is working ‘‘flat out” to cut welfare spending.

Speaking to reporters at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby, when asked if he could confirm what John Healey was reported to have said about planning to cut welfare spending by the next election, Burnham replied:

double quotation mark We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we’re working flat out to that end. Now that we are through the budget, the big next priority in front of us is the publication of the [Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment], long awaited, but it’s coming soon. We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There’s no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible.

Burnham also argued that “crude cuts” on their own would just leave people “in crisis”, requiring more public spending down the line.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was also asked if John Healey’s comments about the EU in a GB interview this morning (see 1 2.14pm ) were out of line with Andy Burnham’s. No, was the answer. The spokesperson said:

double quotation mark The position of the government, and the prime minister and the chancellor, is that a stronger relationship with our closest neighbours is in our national interest.

Healey did not say anything that contradicted Burnham’s views on Brexit . But if Burnham had been asked the GB News questions, he would have stressed the problems with the current EU relationship. Healey, instead, said “we’ve got a Brexit decision” and stressed the importance of making the best of the current arrangements.

No 10 confirms government not setting timetable for when it will cut welfare spending

Downing Street has said John Healey was not committing to cutting welfare spending before the general election in his Today programme interview this morning. (See 9.23am.)

Although one answer he gave to a question could be interpreted as saying that, the PM’s spokesperson said that was not Healey’s message. The spokesperson said:

double quotation mark We’ve never set an arbitrary target or timetable [for when the welfare bill starts to fall]. But both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.

Asked if Healey mis-spoke in his interview, the spokesperson said:

double quotation mark The chancellor is completely in line with what the PM has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and, as I say, we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that.

The spokesperson said the government would be publishing Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment and Stephen Timms’ report on the personal independence payment (Pip), and that these would be followed by a white paper on welfare reform published next year. That will be followed by legislation.

Badenoch claims it's 'astounding' Healey won't commit to cutting welfare bill before general election

Kemi Badenoch has described the Treasury clarification that John Healey is not promising to cut the welfare bill before the general election (see 9.23am ) as “astounding”. In a response on social media , she said:

double quotation mark This is astounding. The government’s own figures show working-age welfare will go up by £60 BILLION by 2030, yet the Treasury has to rush out and correct the Chancellor to say there is no timetable for cutting the benefits bill. Looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading. John Healey couldn’t even find £10 billion to get defence spending to 3% of GDP - the thing he quit over. Don’t let anyone tell you this was a ‘do no harm budget’. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they’ve harmed our national security.

Selling nicotine-free vapes to under-18s banned from today, government says

Selling nicotine-free vapes to children under the age of 18 has become illegal from today, the government has said.

Children were already banned from buying vapes containing nicotine. But, under the Tobacco and Vapes Act, shops across the UK will now be banned from selling nicotine-free vapes, and nicotine pouches, to children.

In an article for the Daily Mirror welcoming the new law, Prof Sir Chris Whitty , the chief medical officer for England, said:

double quotation mark Vaping can be a way to help established adult smokers who are already addicted to nicotine from tobacco to swap to a less dangerous product. Vaping is considered safer than smoking, but that is a low bar. Vapes should therefore never be used by children or non-smokers. Some children have already come to harm from bad reactions to vapes. The long-term health harms of vaping in today’s children will only become clear over time. They are however unlikely to be good; inhaling multiple, often heated, chemicals into the lungs may well do irreversible harm.

According to the Department of Health and Social Care , which has put out a new release about how the ban will operate in England, “more than a million children are estimated to have tried vaping, with more than 370,000 vaping regularly, putting them at a higher risk of developing respiratory illnesses.” Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are also implementing bans.

Healey plays down talk of UK rejoining EU after election, saying he's 'in favour of accepting we've got Brexit decision'

As Peter Walker reports, Andy Burnham has written to cabinet ministers telling them that, as he opens a national debate on improving the UK’s relationship with the EU, he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process”.

John Healey stuck to this in his interviews this morning. But, speaking to GB News, he did hint that he might not be 100% enthusiastic about taking the UK back into the EU single market after the next election.

When Christopher Hope , GB News’ political editor, put it to him that more than two thirds of voters in Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, Healey’s south Yorkshire constituency, voted for Brexit and would not be happy with rejoining the single market, Healey replied:

double quotation mark No, freedom of movement is not on the agenda, and certainly for this parliament it’s ruled out.

Healey said the government would be having “a bigger discussion about how we get a better Brexit deal”. Asked if he would favour joining the EU, with freedom of movement, if that helped the economy, he replied:

double quotation mark No, I’m in favour of accepting that we’ve got a Brexit decision. And I’m in favour of the job we need to do now, which is to make the best of the terms we’ve got.

Healey accepts government faces 'hard decisions' ahead over spending

In his interviews this morning John Healey pushed back a bit against the claims that his plans are based on unrealistic assumptions about spending cuts. (See 11.29am .) Speaking to Bloomberg, he said “hard decisions” would be needed. He said:

double quotation mark My cabinet colleagues are demonstrating that they can also exert fiscal discipline and spending control, and we will take that into the spending review. But the spending review will be framed by the priorities that we set in the 10-year plan for Britain, that’s as it should be. Hard decisions about the top priorities for Britain in the years to come, judgments that then follow about how we fund them.

Healey's longterm government spending plans would require cuts government probably wouldn't accept, IFS says

Here are some more lines from Helen Miller ’s presentation about the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ assessment of the budget. (See 10.45am .)

Miller said higher inflation means John Healey would need at least £17bn to avoid real-terms cuts in some government departments under the long-term spending plans. Echoing a point made by the Resolution Foundation (see 8.36am and 10.21am ), she said:

double quotation mark The chancellor left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms. In the face of higher inflation, this means that the real-terms value of budgets has been cut. Taken at face value, and alongside the inherited plans to slow down spending growth sharply in coming years, that is a big choice. It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review. Avoiding the cuts implied by both higher inflation and tight envelopes could plausibly require a top-up of £17bn in 2030-31. That’s true even before thinking about the £11bn needed to fund defence plans.

She said she did not believe Healey would implement the future spending cuts implied by his departmental spending plans. She said:

double quotation mark I want to be clear that my concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it. I’m also sceptical because I didn’t hear John Healey starting the kind of pitch-rolling that you would expect if he intended to deliver these spending plans. And I’m sceptical because history advises scepticism. When chancellors pencil in tight spending plans in the future, they tend not to deliver.

She criticised Healey for raiding the reserves to fund the defence investment plan. She explained:

double quotation mark I’m grumpy about how the chancellor decided to fund the relatively small hole in the defence investment plan – that’s the plan that gets defence spending to 2.7% of GDP next year and keeps it there until 2029–30. Much of it came from further cuts to the capital budgets of other government departments. Fine. Priorities change. But the rest came from raiding reserves in future years. This is worth drawing out: John Healey has now spent 25% of the capital reserve set aside for the next three years. He’s also spent 40% of the day-to-day reserve. This is categorically not what the reserves are for. Drawing down reserves is another way that the government has reduced its buffer against future shocks.

She said it was “sad” that the government was having to decide who should get energy support based on council tax bands that are based on property values 35 years ago. She said:

double quotation mark It is also sad that, in the time since the last energy price surge, the government hasn’t bothered to invest in the data that would have allowed a package more targeted at those most badly hit by rising energy prices. But here we are.

She said Healey was at risk of needing to put up taxes next year. She said:

double quotation mark I am left with the impression that the chancellor is hoping the economic forecasts improve enough that he can make good on his plan to cut borrowing without having to also make large cuts to public spending or raise taxes. I hope that happens. And it might – a re-opening of the strait of Hormuz or AI-driven productivity growth really could create sunnier skies. But, equally, things could get worse. If they do, the chancellor now has less insurance. A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises.

Healey's new 'founder's relief' tax cut for entrepreneurs 'looks bonkers', says IFS

Helen Miller , director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank, is giving a presentation summing up the IFS’s view of the budget. Arguing that it contained plenty of “bad things” as well as welcome measures, she singled out founders’ relief for particular criticism.

She said:

double quotation mark After years of arguing that business asset disposal relief was a bad idea – and just when I thought the relief was on its last legs – a new, similar relief has popped up. The new founders’ relief looks bonkers. It gives a lower rate of capital gains tax to a small subset of people with large gains. That will include some entrepreneurs that make investments with broader societal benefits – although most of that activity would have happened without the relief. But it will also include people that just got lucky. There are very complex rules around who gets it – rules that will incentivise people to change their behaviour in weird ways simply to be able to get the relief. I could go on. But the punchline is that this looks to me like yet another tax break for a chosen group with little economic reasoning behind it.

Tories overtake Reform UK in 'poll of polls' tracker

Since the start of 2025 Reform UK has been ahead of the Conservative party in the Politico poll of polls , a tracker which averages how the political parties are in surveys carried out by all the main polling organisations. Different polling companies use different methods, and so the poll of polls provides a reliable overview. Other poll of poll trackers are available, but Politico’s may be the most widely read in Westminster.

And today it has good news for the Conservatives. For the first time since early 2025, they have regained their lead over Reform UK.

How 2020s are set to be worst decade, by far, since 1960s for rising living standards, according to Resolution Foundation

The Resolution Foundation has now published its full 48-page report on the budget. Some of its main arguments were covered earlier. (See 8.36am .)

Here are five charts from the report illustrating five of its main arguments.

1) The amount the government is spending paying interest on its debt is “high and rising”, the report says. It says:

double quotation mark Debt interest spending is now forecast to reach £147bn in 2029-30, £13bn more than in March. This leaves debt interest spending at 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30 (and peaking marginally higher at 4.14 per cent in 2031-32, the highest on record since 1956-57) and above the total expected spend on universal credit, Housing Benefit and Child Benefit combined in that year.

2) The 2020s are set to be the worst decade, by far, for more than half a century for rising living standards, the report says.

double quotation mark The 2020s are on course to have the lowest growth in incomes of any decade on record when measured using Real Household Disposable Income (RHDI). RHDI is projected to rise by just 1.4 per cent in total over the decade (equivalent to £400 in 2026-27 prices), one-tenth of the growth rate achieved in the 2010s (which itself was the second-worst decade on record). Income growth this decade is set to be much weaker than GDP growth because of rising taxes and import prices.

3) Labour’s cost of living support package benefits the rich almost as much as the poor, the report says.

double quotation mark Taken altogether, the Government’s £4.4bn cost of living package for 2025-26 and 2026-27 is poorly targeted. As Figure 8 makes clear, support is very widely spread. The Household Energy Payment goes to up to 20 million households in England, which are dispersed across the income distribution (87 per cent of the bottom half of the income distribution and 73 per cent of the top live in Council Tax bands A-D). The VAT cut and the Fuel Duty delay are not targeted at all. Taken together, we estimate that 52 per cent of the whole cost of living package will benefit the poorest half of the income distribution this year and next, with the other 48 per cent going to the top half (equivalent to an average £158 for poorer households, compared to £144 for richer households).

4) But, overall, the tax and benefit changes since the government took power have been progressive, the report says.

double quotation mark We estimate that annual incomes will, on average, be £320 higher for households in the bottom quintile in 2029- 30, compared to £2,000 lower for those in the top quintile as a result of the Starmer and Burnham governments’ measures. This is largely the result of policies announced before this budget: the repeal of the two-child limit and the commitment to uprate the universal credit standard allowance at a higher rate than inflation for four years, both introduced from April 2026.

5) All government spending departments apart from defence, health and education are likely to face cuts in spending per head from the end of this decade under current plans, the report says.

Healey denies postponing difficult decisions on welfare

John Healey has denied postponing difficult decisions on the welfare system, insisting the government is making changes “now”.

Thinktanks and opposition parties have made this claim. But, when this was put to Healey in an interview on GB News, he replied:

double quotation mark This was a broken system. And two years ago we started putting back in place face-to-face assessments. We’ve changed terms of universal credit, so people don’t have to brand themselves as too sick to work. So, those are changes we’re making now. But in the long run, as I’ve argued, and the prime minister has said, too, we have to bring the cost of benefits down.

Treasury says Healey hasn't committed to cutting welfare bill before election, claiming interview answer misinterpreted

John Healey is rowing back from his answer in an interview in the Today programme implying he wanted welfare spending to go down before the next general election. According to Chris Mason , the BBC’s political editor, Treasury sources are saying his words have been over-interpreted.

This relates to what Healey said in an interview with Nick Robinson for the Today programme. It was broadcast this morning, but recorded yesterday, and the BBC has written it up in a story on its website headlined: “Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election”.

For the record, here is the key exchange.

double quotation mark Robinson: Let’s take welfare if we could. £19bn up in the year ahead. That’s the entire police budget for England and Wales. That’s the entire annual defence equipment budget. And yet in your speech you said, well, we’ve got a couple of reports coming next month, then we’ll have a white paper, which in non-Westminster jargon means a consultation, then you’ll have some legislation, then you’ll have a row in the Labour party. You’re not going to make any of these cuts before the next election, are you? Healey: Well first, I’ve said clearly, the prime minister said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures. We do have a big report, two big reports being produced next month, that will help us map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run. We are in fact reducing and have been over the last two years the rate of increase in the welfare bill compared to the previous period – I’m afraid to say – of a broken system the Conservatives put in place. We’re bringing back and have brought back face to face assessments which they axed for instance. We’ve been changing universal credits so people aren’t branding themselves as too sick to work in order to make that system work better. Robinson: But you’re reducing the rate of increase in welfare spending chancellor aren’t you? But the OBR’s forecast is that £1 in every £8 will be spent on welfare by 2030 or thereabouts. You’ve got to make cuts, haven’t you? Healey: This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The prime minister’s been clear about it …. Robinson: Briefly, because I want to give you the chance to talk about other things – there will be cuts in welfare before the election? Healey: There will be there will be a reduction in the benefits bill . We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill and I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters who at the moment have been written off by previous governments.

The answer highlighted in bold is what gave the BBC its story. Healey paused slightly between the first “there will be” and the second “there will be” and it would be perfectly reasonable to interpret it as:

double quotation mark There will be. [Direct answer to Robinson’s question.] There will be a reduction in the benefits bill [etc etc – Healey expanding on the answer.]

But the Treasury is implying what he meant was:

double quotation mark There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill [Healey simply repeating three words as he launches into more general answer, not answering Robinson directly, but just explaining the government’s approach.]

Reasonable people could interpret is either way. But Mason said the Treasury had told him the first interpretation was not accurate, and that if Healey really wanted to commit to getting cutting the benefits bill before the general election, he would have announced that in the budget.

Given that Alan Milburn himself has said that his plans to tackle youth unemployment may require more spending upfront in return for savings later, and given that welfare reforms often take most of a decade to roll out, it does seem unlikely that Healey intended to say the benefits bill would be cut before the election.

But, as Mason pointed out on the Today programme, “correcting” this story means the Treasury is implicitly saying benefit spending won’t go down before the election – which is very helpful to the Tories and Reform UK.

Healey accused by Resolution Foundation of ‘complete failure’ to target energy bill support at those most in need

Good morning. The day after the budget is often the moment when big initiatives announced by the chancellor the day before with a flourish start to unravel as experts pore over the small print. There is not much of that happening this morning – mainly because John Healey did not have any really big initiatives up his sleeve. Compared with a normal budget, his tax and spending initiatives were mostly relatively minor . That means that the opposition parties have been struggling to find things to attack, and so instead they have resorted to criticising Healey for what he did not do: slash welfare (the Tory/Reform UK solution), or join the EU’s single market (the Lib Dems’).

Healey has given interviews to all the main broadcasters, which are playing out this morning, but they were recorded last night and they don’t have any sensational new revelations. As Rowena Mason reports, one of the top lines was Healey saying he would cut welfare spending before the election.

But there were other lines in the interviews too. I will be posting all the highlights this morning.

The two main public spending thinktanks, the Institute for Fiscal Studies and the Resolution Foundation , are both publishing reports assessing the budget this morning. The RF has issued a news release with its main findings and its assessment of the overall economic impact of the budget measures highlights three problems.

It accuses Healey of a “complete failure” to target help with energy bills at those most in need. It says:

double quotation mark The poorest half of households will gain £158 on average from cost of living support this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half – highlighting a complete failure to target help at those who need it most.

It says long-term public spending plans imply a return to austerity. It says:

double quotation mark Tight spending plans beyond 2028-29 imply departmental budgets will take more of the strain in the future. But if the 3% defence target is met and real health spending continues to grow at 2.6%, pencilled-in spending totals imply that funding for 13 ‘unprotected’ departments will fall to just 4.7% of GDP by 2031-32, close to the post-austerity historic low.

It says people will get poorer between now and the end of the parliament. It says:

double quotation mark Median real annual disposable incomes for working age households are set to grow by a paltry £600 over the course of the parliament. Worse still, those gains are already behind us. Between now (2026-27) and the end of the parliament (2028-29), typical incomes are forecast to fall in total by £1,050 (3 per cent).

This is one reason why so many people continue to think Andy Burnham will call an election next spring (before the electorate feels the full misery of getting poorer) – despite Burnham yesterday saying he would not hold one within the next 12 months.

Here is the agenda for the day.

9am: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Ruth Curtice, head of the Resolution Foundation , speak at an event where the RF is presenting its budget analysis.

9.30am: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

10.30am: Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies , presents the IFS’s budget analysis.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 11.30am: MPs resume the budget debate in the Commons.

Lunchtime: Andy Burnham is on a visit to a Rolls-Royce factory in the Midlands where he is speaking to the media.
