Healey: 'There will be a reduction in the benefits bill'

Published 29 October 2026, 05:57 GMT

The Treasury is disputing that Chancellor John Healey suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next general election.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election, with one suggesting Healey was explicitly attempting to avoid that impression being left.

This suggests, instead, that ministers are not committed to cutting the benefits bill by the next election.

The chancellor told Today: "I have said clearly and the prime minister has said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don't do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures."

He said two "big reports" next month would help the government "map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run" and the government has "been reducing the rate of increase in the welfare bill".

Healey said the current system was "unsustainable" and the government had a "moral duty" to help the almost one million young people out of work, education or training.

He said young people would be expected to take up offers of work or training "and that's the way we can take welfare bills down in the long term".

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 22 hours ago

What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out Published 19 hours ago

Asked whether would be cuts in welfare before the next election, the chancellor said: "There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way and we'll do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.

"And I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters that have been written off by previous governments."

A review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn will be published in November.

The government is then expected to respond by the end of the year and publish a policy document setting out proposals, and legislation next year.

The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare", while Reform UK said the Budget did not address the "ballooning" benefits bill. Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.

Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.

Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.

The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 , and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

'Out-of-control welfare system'

The chancellor's remarks came after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the benefits bill was "going up by tens of billions of pounds because this government has put welfare first".

She said the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system", adding that the Budget was "not bold enough".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said welfare reform "needs to be done right", adding this should involve "cutting the bill by helping people into work and giving people the care and support they need so that they can work".

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, noted the government still has "many difficult decisions" to take after not fleshing out several big issues, including disability benefits and support for young people.

The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices

A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices.

The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press . The ship has a 650-passenger capacity.

The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”.

“Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives over the next 60 days.”

The ship is now docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with a departure date still unclear.

The price of fuel across the world has jumped since the start of the US war on Iran earlier this year. The ship’s operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800.

The strait of Hormuz, which transports much of the world’s oil, has effectively been closed since 28 February, the beginning of the war. Oil prices climbed to above $117 a barrel this month.

One resident on the ship, Randy Cassingham, wrote in a blogpost that he only discovered the cruise route’s cancellation after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship on Monday morning.

“It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote. “It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.”

Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health.

Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. Despite the issues, however, Larson said she did not regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” she said. “From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising.”

Our inflation explorer tracks how prices have risen – or fallen – since 2022

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

It has been nearly five years since inflation crashed on to Australia’s shores, as a rebounding post-Covid economy collided with a world of constrained supply.

The global cost-of-living crisis – or affordability crisis, as the Americans call it – has shaped our world from 2022 onwards.

It was also the year that Russia invaded Ukraine, triggering the first of two global energy shocks.

The second energy shock, of course, arrived this February, when the United States and Israel decided to go to war with Iran.

It is in no small part due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, and the associated surge in fuel costs, that inflation in Australia jumped to 4.3% in the year to September.

While we remain focused on the dramas of 2026, it’s worth taking a longer-term view on how cost-of-living pressures have accumulated in recent years.

For example, fuel costs have risen by more than 20% in the past year, but over the longer term they have matched overall inflation (which is still a pretty big increase).

Our inflation explorer tracks all the categories included in the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ consumer price index.

Our interactive chart shows inflation has climbed 23% since the end of 2021.

But which goods and services have soared by more than that over recent years, and which haven’t?

You can explore the data at your own pace but here are some highlights.

Bills, bills, bills

No surprise that electricity is among the costs that have increased the most. Household power bills are up by 35% since the start of 2022.

The chart shows the zigzagging line as federal and state government subsidies have turned on and off. It is clear also that these subsidies, while welcome at the time, did nothing to change the upwards trend. Relatedly, gas is also up 49%.

Another cost that is hard to avoid is insurance, and the chart shows premiums have surged by 46% in nearly five years. Rental costs are 27% higher. Homebuilding costs are 36% higher.

Postal services are up 40%. Speaking of essentials, supermarket staples such as oil and eggs have increased by more than 40%, and bread, milk and fruit prices are up more than 30% in five years.

On the upside, chicken and vegetables have increased by less than inflation.

Not all bad news

The chart shows that, generally, the lowest price increases over recent years are for non-essentials.

Household items such as glassware, tableware and household utensils are actually cheaper. Electrical items, toasters and so forth, are on average no more expensive now than they were at the end of 2021.

Women’s clothing is just 7% more expensive, and men’s only 4%.

The biggest price decline has been in public transport fees – down 5%, presumably thanks to state and territory government decisions.

Perhaps the most surprising result is that childcare costs, while they have been rising of late, are only up 7% since the end of 2021.

stories.title: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
stories.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
While earnings are rising, forecasters predict that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes

Published 28 October 2026

John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 22 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 3 minutes ago

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

stories.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
stories.summary: The chancellor targets the cost of living amid global economic turmoil but opposition parties say he has not been bold enough.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 28 October 2026

Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

These include:

One-off £100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it

Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills

Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July

Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

Healey announces £100 energy bill help for millions and raises taxes on banks and some savers

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 22 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 3 minutes ago

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures Published 22 hours ago

As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.

But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.

Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.

But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.

In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".

In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.

"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: What are the key points from the Budget and how will it be funded?

Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.

The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".

But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn , into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments , had been published, with legislation to follow next year.

The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.

Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.

But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.

"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.

"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."

The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".

Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".

"Scrapping standing charges on gas and a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over £400 in January," she added.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".

He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

stories.title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
stories.summary: The point at which you start to pay tax, and the point where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax have been frozen for three more years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2025

Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.

John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.

The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.

But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.

Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.

It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.

The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.

Who is affected by frozen thresholds?

They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.

By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.

The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.

However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax .

The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary , external .

National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 3 minutes ago

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 22 hours ago

How does it work?

Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.

So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.

If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.

Will I pay the higher rate?

As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.

An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.

If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.

As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.

If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.

Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.

The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.

Will I be better off after 2031?

Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.

Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.

However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.

How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.

There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

stories.title: Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
stories.summary: The prime minister has denied speculation from some opposition parties that he will go to the country in spring 2027.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The prime minister was asked about speculation from the Tories and Reform UK

Published 28 October 2026

Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.

The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.

Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."

He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.

She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."

She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".

"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."

Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.

He has since outlined a number of ambitions , which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.

One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.

On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".

The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.

Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

stories.title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
stories.summary: The reduction in public spending will go towards paying for the Defence Investment Plan.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Members of the Finnish army and British army on a training exercise on Nato's border with Russia

Published 28 October 2026

Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.

The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag.

The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."

Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".

He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.

Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.

Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped .

Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.

"He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.

The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.

Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".

Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".

He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."

Former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson told the BBC the Budget was "pretty good news for defence generally" but warned there would be "battles ahead with the spending departments" to reach the 3% target.

Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.

In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.

Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.

"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."

In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".

The chancellor said this would include:

starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resources

increasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnerships

directing the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put £5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.

"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role Published 16 October

Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace' Published 16 October

Burnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine Published 14 October

In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.

The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.

A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.

Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".

He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."

Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."

The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

Published 28 September 2026

Chancellor John Healey has set out the government's tax and spending plans in his Budget – the first since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Here is a summary of the main points.

LIVE: Follow all the Budget coverage

One-off £100 payment for up to 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England to help deal with rising energy bills, with equivalent funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

Standing charges – fixed daily fees customers pay regardless of usage – to be removed from household gas bills in England, Scotland and Wales, with costs added to the unit rate instead

VAT cut on electricity bills extended to July

A green levy - the Gas Shipper Obligation to fund hydrogen projects - to be removed from energy bills and put on to general taxation

Freeze on fuel duty extended again to July

Import taxes to be removed on more than 100 food products, including gherkins and marmalade, as well as kerosene and fertilisers

A 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work made permanent, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that distance

A new scheme taking 25% off electricity bills for 10,000 energy-intensive businesses to launch in April, with payments backdated for energy costs this year

From April 2027, landlords will face a further 2% in income tax on rental profits

An extra 2% tax on income from savings and property rental from April

Amount people can put into tax-free cash Isas (Individual Savings Accounts) to remain at £20,000 a year, with plans to lower the limit to £12,000 for under-65s scrapped

Surcharge banks pay on their profits to rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months, starting in January

Threshold at which High Street shops start paying business rates in England to be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level

Adult games centres and vape shops will no longer qualify for certain business rates relief

Taxes on gambling machines with stakes over £1 to rise from 20% to 25%

Online marketplaces like Amazon, eBay and Temu to be made responsible for collecting VAT owed by sellers using their platforms

New, flat-rate state pension to rise by £488 a year from April – equivalent to 3.9% - under the triple lock policy , with old basic state pension to rise by £374.40

A new tax-free allowance for low-income pensioners, to ensure those with income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax

Legal minimum wage to rise by 3.9% in April

Unpaid carers will no longer lose their entire Carer's Allowance if they earn more than £204 a week after tax, with a taper rate introduced instead

Parental pay extended to self-employed fathers and parents in same-sex couples

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 3 minutes ago

The one thing that didn't change that will affect your pay the most Published 21 hours ago

A further £432m has been added to the initiative to end rough sleeping by Christmas

New scheme to help first-time buyers in England purchase a home, offering government-backed loans to households earning less than £110,000 , or £140,000 inside London

A new First Time Buyer ISA to be introduced from April 2029, to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save a deposit for their first home

Lifetime ISA holders buying a property above the £450,000 cap will pay a reduced withdrawal charge of 20%, down from 25%

An extra £1bn for social and affordable housing in England , taking total funding for the 10-year programme to more than £40bn

An extra £432m for a programme aimed at giving every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas

All business rates to be retained locally by the end of the decade, with mayors to keep 20% of revenue from next year

A share of income tax receipts to go to mayors from 2028

Regional bodies and mayors in England to get greater powers over spending, starting with £285m next year for things like housing, transport and High Streets

Government to work with mayors to design a £1.5bn borrowing facility, enabling investment in larger projects

The chancellor promised an uplift in defence spending by 2030

Defence Investment Plan to be fully funded through a further 1% cut to capital budgets of other government departments , after Sir Keir Starmer only committed £10.3bn for the £15bn plan

Details of how the government will meet a Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 to be set out at next year's Spending Review, with a target date for 3% in 2030

Extra £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine

More than £600m of investment in projects related to artificial intelligence (AI), including an extra £120m for the UK's AI Security Institute and £100m for a national AI Biosecurity Lab

A £7m fund to explore a possible future bid to hold the Olympics and Paralympics in northern England

Fund to tackle misogyny in schools, at work and in communities to get £15m

Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) predicts the UK economy will grow by 1.2% this year, up from a previous estimate of 1.1%

Growth then expected to slow to 1% next year, a downgrade from the watchdog's previous forecast of 1.6%, before lifting back to 1.6% in 2028

Inflation – the rate prices rise – is predicted to average 3.1% this year and then 3.4% in 2027, a hike on previous forecasts, before declining to the government's 2% target in 2028

Government borrowing is predicted to be higher than previously expected in every year of the latest forecast

stories.title: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
stories.summary: The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the Brexit deal at a summit in Brussels next month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister's Questions focused on Andy Burnham's Brexit stance

Published 28 October 2026

Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.

The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.

He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.

Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.

"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.

"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.

"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.

"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.

It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.

Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion Published 2 days ago

Burnham pledges not to 're-run' Brexit arguments Published 18 May

Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days Published 2 days ago

Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.

"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."

Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.

"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.

At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.

Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.

"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.

He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".

"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.

"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."

Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures
stories.summary: The chancellor has had to grapple with a mix of public finances and household finances being a mess.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor John Healey unveiled his Budget on Wednesday

Published 28 October 2026

This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.

Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book , external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published , external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.

The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.

But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.

This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address – but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.

Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value – and others that some will likely curse.

There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.

When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT – the big revenue generators – they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary.

That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.

More on this story

Live: Healey announces £100 energy bill help for millions and raises taxes on banks

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 22 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 3 minutes ago

Chancellor begins to deliver his first Budget Published 1 day ago

The central challenge for Healey, which he shares with his recent predecessors, is the public finances are in a mess and so are the personal finances of so, so many households.

And there is a recurring sense of déjà vu in the language of the OBR. "The UK's economic and fiscal position remains very challenging," it says, with a splash of understatement, adding that "there have been further adverse developments" this year with in the conflict in the Middle East.

As for what happens, next, well, frankly, who on earth knows. Or, as the OBR puts it: "The outlook for the economy and the public finances is uncertain, with significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability."

The Budget book argues that "the UK economy is showing signs of resilience" but it is also true that the national debt, tax burden, inflation and interest rates are high, going up or both – and there could yet be further economic shocks that make things worse.

What happens, for instance, in the Middle East, once the mid term elections are done in America and the result of the Israeli general election is clear?

In short, the chancellor felt constrained in his capacity to act and his capacity to make a noticeable positive difference is perhaps constrained even more so – because any intervention, even expensive ones, may merely make a grim situation a bit less bad , rather than things actually feeling better.

Mitigating the bad is arguably a noble political aim, but it costs money and potentially comes with little political upside.

What are the standout points from the Budget?

Instead there is this fleet of smaller measures that the government will hope gives their MPs something to try to sell – while acknowledging that they are not world changing.

Luke Tryl, the UK Director of the More in Common think tank, says: "The softly populist tone of this budget is likely to land well with the public. The Chancellor targeted groups the public have little sympathy with - banks, landlords, gambling companies and vape shops - and turned it into cost-of-living support, rate relief for small businesses and ensuring the state pension isn't taxed."

He adds: "Crucially, the chancellor may have avoided the biggest potential trap of the Budget - being seen to offer energy support for those on benefits and incurring the ire of the squeezed middle, who think they work hard but are left to fend for themselves.

"Instead, by offering support to all of those on Council Tax bands A to D, he is able to reassure them that the government will support them too."

The reaction of the opposition parties, from a range of different political perspectives, amounts to a critique that this Budget was thin.

The government counters that it is one piece in the emerging jigsaw of detail from the new-ish prime minister and his chancellor – with a plan help young people into work and cut benefits before Christmas, alongside a big picture sense of what the UK's long term relationship with the European Union could look like and a 10 year vision from Andy Burnham.

In summary, this felt like a cautious Budget. One critical friend of the government suggested to me this would be a "Mr Sensible Budget" – their hope and expectation that it might be shorn of bells and whistles, but shorn of timebombs too. Let's see.

stories.title: How much is the minimum wage going up by?
stories.summary: What are the National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage, and how much are they worth?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 May 2019

The official minimum rates of pay will rise for 2.3 million workers on 1 April.

The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage. They will both go up by 3.9% next year.

The rates apply across the UK.

What is the National Living Wage rate?

From 1 April 2027, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage will be paid £13.21p per hour, up 50p from the current £12.71 an hour.

For someone working full time (35 hours a week), that means an increase of £910 to their gross annual earnings, according to the Treasury.

What is the National Minimum Wage rate?

The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds will rise to £11.27 an hour from 1 April, up from £10.85. For someone working full time, that means an increase of £760 to their gross annual earnings.

The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds is also rising by 3.9%, increasing from £8 an hour to £8.31.

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

What is the apprentice rate and how much is it worth?

There are different rates of pay for apprentices , external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in.

Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group. This is currently £8 an hour but will rise by 3.9% to £8.31 in April.

Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount.

But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age.

What is an apprenticeship and how much is the pay? Published 20 August

Who doesn't qualify for the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage?

Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage.

This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners.

People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme.

These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate.

Do employers have to pay the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage?

Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees.

The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour.

Calculator: Am I getting the right wage? , external

If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website , external .

You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas , external .

What happens if employers don't pay the right wage?

Any employer not paying the correct amount can be penalised by HMRC.

In March 2026, the government said that 389 employers had been fined around £12.6m for failing to pay staff properly , external .

They must also repay the missing £7.3m to the around 60,000 workers who were underpaid.

Firm named included the Nursery chain Busy Bees , Norwich City Football Club, Hays Travel and Costa Coffee.

What is the Real Living Wage and how much is it?

The Real Living Wage , external is an unofficial hourly rate of pay which is overseen by the Living Wage Foundation charity, who say it is set at a rate to meet the cost of living.

It increases every October.

Some firms choose to pay the Real Living Wage, but it is not mandatory.

According to the charity almost 500,000 employees working for nearly 17,000 firms receive the voluntary rate of pay.

In October 2026, the foundation said the UK rate would increase by 4.8% to £14.10 an hour, while the London Living Wage for workers in the capital would go up by 4.4% to £15.45.

The Living Wage Foundation says the rate is worth over £2,700 more per year than the legal minimum wage in the UK, and over £5,300 more in London.

Departure of Lagarde, seen as candidate to take over World Economic Forum, comes as eurozone struggles with weak growth and inflation

Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is stepping down nine months early, ending months of speculation about her future.

The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday morning that Lagarde would step down as its president on 7 February 2027. Her term was scheduled to run until the end of October next year.

The ECB’s governing council thanked Lagarde warmly and gave her a longstanding ovation, as it met to set interest rates across the eurozone.

In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a “great pride and huge privilege” to serve at the ECB. “I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” she added.

Lagarde has been seen as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.

Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.

The European Council appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone. It left interest rates on hold on Thursday, but cautioned that the rise in energy costs poses upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook.

French ⁠president Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday ⁠that Lagarde’s ​succession at the helm of ⁠the European Central Bank must ⁠be prepared in “an orderly ​and ‌balanced way” ‌with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action ‌during her time at the ​ECB.

Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.

“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”

after newsletter promotion

Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic . During her tenure the ECB has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict and Donald Trump’s trade war.

Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

Video appears to show Mao Zedong called a ‘dictator’

Dongpeng and Mengniu end deals with the player

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

after newsletter promotion

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”

stories.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
stories.summary: US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.

Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.

Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.

One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.

Mapping the risks

The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.

Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims , and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

The index suggests that the risk to cables is highest around Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, partly because of China’s claim of sovereignty over Taiwan but also because subsea cables linking the region to the United States must pass through shallow water with busy shipping lanes.

Among the 10 trans-Pacific cables identified as being most at risk, several are still under development with significant ownership stakes from US companies. These include the TPU project, owned by Google, the ORCA cable, owned by Meta, and the E2A cable, co-owned by Verizon along with firms in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. All three of these projects had risk scores in the top five.

The report authors warn that any serious disruption to a single trans-Pacific cable could “risk overwhelming current available capacity on direct routings between the United States, Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, forcing data onto slower, less direct routes.”

An even greater disruption involving multiple cables, potentially during a geopolitical crisis involving Taiwan, could “significantly reduce headroom and even overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity as a whole,” with communications between the United States and Indo-Pacific region having to reroute through other cables across the globe. That could have major economic consequences for Internet communications, cloud services, and financial trading.

Dual-use technologies and survey tracks

This comes as the world’s major powers continue to build up their fleets of military submarines and undersea drones, along with further developing and deploying dual-use technologies, like undersea cable cutters that could either be used for repair or sabotage.

China has also deployed a fleet of research vessels equipped with seabed-mapping technologies near trans-Pacific undersea cables, according to a separate report published in October 2026 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a think tank based in Washington, DC.

The CSIS analysts found that China-flagged research ships stood out as outliers in the amount of time spent near subsea infrastructure. They analyzed the movements of more than 200 research ships from multiple nations between 2020 and 2025.

This pattern involving Chinese vessels stood out even when compared with the generally high activity of US and Russian research ships on the high seas. Several Chinese ships spent much of their time performing survey-style tracks near undersea cables rather than checking out regions known for undersea mineral deposits.

One of the most surprising findings involved the China-linked research vessel Ke Xue that made a journey to the Bering Sea between Russia and the United States. While likely checking out a US military base in the Aleutian Islands, the ship also began doing “survey-like movements” near a Russian government-owned cable called Polar Express.

That likely indicates China’s interest in mapping Russia’s subsea telecommunications infrastructure, even though China and Russia have maintained strong economic and military ties, according to the CSIS analysts.

Chinese-owned fishing boats and cargo vessels have been involved in several notable cable-cutting incidents in recent years, especially near Taiwan. One incident in 2025 led to the first case of Taiwan’s government convicting and sentencing a Chinese captain to three years in prison, after his ship dropped anchor and performed a zigzag pattern that damaged the Tai-Peng 3 cable linking Taiwan to the offshore islands of Penghu.

The broader threat

The Pacific is not the only region where undersea cables face growing danger. In recent years, both Russian- and Chinese-linked ships have been investigated for causing damage to subsea communications cables, power cables, and pipelines in the Baltic Sea. These incidents typically involved ships that dragged their anchors over unusually long periods of time.

On October 21, The Telegraph published an analysis showing more than 500 incidents involving Russia’s fleet of fishing boats loitering near crucial undersea cables connecting the UK to the rest of the world, with some vessels following the routes of the undersea cables. Reuters reporting also recently revealed that NATO countries had confronted Russian submarines that were practicing how to disable undersea cables using a new type of technology in Arctic waters near Norway earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Iran has repeatedly threatened to charge fees to US tech companies for the undersea Internet cables running beneath the contested Strait of Hormuz and has prepared plans to attack them —another consequence of the wider war that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026.

For a big-picture perspective on why the world has become more dangerous for the Internet’s undersea backbone, Ars recently interviewed Elisabeth Braw , author of the book Undersea War .

This story was updated on October 28, 2026 with additional details about how a China-linked research vessel unexpectedly spent some time apparently surveying a Russian subsea cable.
