stories.body:
Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Briefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crerar

Editorial: Budget’s bold ambitions and welcome first steps

John Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis.

In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices.

But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest.

In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.

But with households facing soaring energy prices, and mortgage bills rising amid higher interest rates, Healey offered a £100 cost-of-living payout, which will be sent to all English households in council tax bands A-D.

It formed the centrepiece of a cost of living package, which he said would “take the pressure off in the coldest months, and see people through to the spring”.

The £2.6bn cost of the £100 giveaway includes funding for the Scottish and Welsh governments, which Healey said he hoped they would use to implement a similar scheme.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said.

But the government’s independent forecaster warned households face a “grim picture” on living standards, as it slashed the outlook for the economy in 2027 and said there was “virtually no growth” in disposable income for households.

Healey also came under fire for an unexpected 2p increase in tax rates for income earned on property or savings. As well as hitting savers and landlords, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it risks “leading to a steady rise in rents”, by deterring landlords from the market and cutting supply, as well as passing on costs to tenants.

Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation thinktank, criticised the £100 handout, arguing it would have been better to give more generous support to the poorest consumers.

“The chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise,” she said.

As expected, the chancellor also cancelled fuel tax rises planned by Rachel Reeves, and extended the VAT cut on electricity prices previously announced to next summer.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

The cost of the household support measures will be met by a doubling of the additional levy banks pay on their profits, to 6%; as well as the higher taxes on income from property and savings.

The additional bank tax will only last for 15 months and marked a less significant rise than some in the industry had feared. Banks’ share prices were among the highest risers in the blue chip FTSE 100 index on Wednesday.

Laura Suter, director of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: “Savers will be hit with another hefty tax rise on their savings interest, adding to the squeeze on their savings over the past few years.”

She added that the higher tax on rental income “could be passed on to tenants, with rent hikes a potential lever for landlords to mitigate any increase in tax”.

“Equally, we could see yet more landlords selling up, in favour of investing their money in other assets that have lower taxes and less government tinkering,” she said.

The New Economics Foundation thinktank accused Healey of failing to be bold enough. Hannah Peaker, its deputy chief executive, said: “As households prepare to be hit by a wave of price rises this winter, the chancellor has shown the right instincts but not yet the right scale.

“The £100 support with energy bills will provide some welcome relief, but the chancellor could have been braver in the face of what we are up against.”

after newsletter promotion

Energy provider EDF predicts that the Ofgem price cap – which determines consumer bills – is set to go up by £466 in January . And despite Healey’s promise of a “breathing space,” in the teeth of the crisis, official forecasts published by the OBR alongside the budget pointed to a challenging winter.

Presenting the forecasts, the OBR’s David Miles highlighted a “pretty grim picture” for household finances, as inflation rises to almost 4%.

Even by 2030-31, it only expects real disposable household incomes – its favoured measure of living standards – to be 2% higher than before the Covid pandemic. It now expects anaemic economic growth of 1% next year, about half a percentage point lower than expected in March.

Healey said higher inflation and interest rates had hit the government’s finances too, ratcheting up the government’s interest bill by £14bn this year alone, but promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules.

The OBR said Healey would meet the most important rule – to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – with a diminished headroom of £15bn by the target date of 2029-30, against the £24bn Rachel Reeves had built up in the spring.

Borrowing is scheduled to be higher than expected in the short term, but the chancellor promised to rebuild the buffer against the rules to £22bn by the end of the five-year forecast period.

“That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said. Bond markets appeared unruffled by the higher-than-expected borrowing.

The deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, to argue Burnham was keeping his options open on an early general election.

Burnham doubled down on his promise not to call one, however, telling reporters on Wednesday that he could rule one out for at least 12 months. “I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects. I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them.”

Badenoch said Britain had “overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed”, and criticised Healey for delayed decisions on defence spending and welfare cuts. Healey has said he will tackle welfare after reports from Alan Milburn on youth unemployment and Sir Stephen Timms on disability benefits, expected next month.

Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that by sticking to the tight spending plans bequeathed by Reeves, Healey could be storing up trouble for the spending review due next year.

“History warns us to be sceptical of tight spending plans in later years of the forecast. Next year’s spending review will be a crunch point, and looks very tough for many departments, whose budgets will be squeezed by higher inflation forecasts,” she said.

“The plans for overall spending set out in the budget mean that spending choices at next year’s spending review will be much harder than those made so far this parliament.”

Buried in the budget was a hint at an easing of some migration restrictions, including some industries that will be allowed to lower the salary thresholds for visas to allow companies across the country to hire international talent.

Among the winners was London mayor Lord Sadiq Khan , who received new powers to extend the Bakerloo line in London and a pledge that cross-Channel trains will now also stop at Stratford International in east London. There was also cash to explore hosting the Olympics in “a northern city” – and former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham may have a candidate city in mind.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Businesses in Devon and Cornwall said there were both positives and negatives to the budget

Published 22 minutes ago

Tourism and hospitality leaders have been reacting to this week's Budget.

Among the headlines in chancellor John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday were a £100 payment to help millions of households with energy bills, a VAT cut on electricity bills and a freeze on fuel duty, both extended to July.

It also announced Devon would get an elected mayor in 2028 white Cornwall was included as the only area on a pathway to become a Foundation Strategic Authority.

Sue Jewell, chair of South East Cornwall Tourism Association and a holiday accommodation provider, said the budget "gave with one hand and took with the other".

As part of the Budget legal minimum wage is to rise by 3.9% in April

Jewell said: "I think it's tricky because actually I would believe that quite a lot of people in our business anyway pay over the minimum wage just to retain staff.

"However because of the cost we've cut back on staff.

"Which is sad really because it's local people who could be having local jobs."

Dr Harry Pitts, senior lecturer in Politics at the University of Exeter's Cornwall Campus, said the £100 energy payment was one of the "small things to make life a little easier for some households in the immediate period".

Anyone living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment", funded by extra tax on banks.

'Scary for business'

The Budget announced the threshold at which high street shops start paying business rates in England was to be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level.

Toby Parkins, interim ceo at the Cornwall Chamber of Commerce, said he predicted this would benefit about 900 extra businesses in Cornwall.

"For the small business that is a big win," he said.

Helen Wylde-Archibald, from the Devon Chamber of Commerce, said she "welcomed some stability".

"The last two have been a bit scary for business," she said, referring to previous Budgets.

She added: "It doesn't necessarily give us all the conditions we want for full growth and strong growth, but the main thing was there was no broad base business tax rises and fuel duty remains frozen until July."

She said she didn't think there was enough in the way of announcements of more support for farming and food, and this had "an impact on the rural economy".

'Just so sad'

James Kittow, from Butcher & Grazier in Cornwall, said: "It just seems like we've been forgotten again.

"We're an industry that is ready, willing and able to help the country produce the food for the nation."

He added there was no change on inheritance tax for farmers. Since April, inherited farming assets worth more than £2.5m face 20% inheritance tax

"I'm looking to plan for a succession... we want to keep farming, we want to keep doing what we love doing but if we're going to get hit on the other end of it then it does make you think twice about what is all this for, and it's just so sad for the future farmers that want to come into the trade," he said.

'Existing property'

Andrea Drew, managing director at Lander Mortgage Services, said the key announcement relating to housing was a scheme for first time buyers, and a a "First Time Buyer Isa".

This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

"The only negative I would say... on new builds, the housing market isn't just all about new builds, it's about existing property... because not everybody wants to have a new build property," she said.

She added: "The other thing was about the increase in tax for landlords so, they're increasing the tax by 4%."

She said she'd seen landlords who decided to sell their property because of the amount of tax but tenants couldn't afford to buy the homes.

"What tenants need is more homes to choose from, not fewer, and they can't solve the housing shortage by destroying people who are providing the housing," she said.

stories.title: Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better
stories.summary: Everyone knows, or should, that perfect (balanced, targeted, transparent, swift and swiftly appealable) content moderation at scale is impossible. That doesn’t mean powerful social platforms don’t have to try to get at least reasonably close, especially when access to good information can have a profound effect on political participation and speech. That’s why so many people, including the Meta Oversight Board , criticized Meta for suspending a major political Instagram account for hours during a huge early voting push on October 17; and for allegedly boosting one candidate in Brazil’s recent presidential election. Meta denies deliberate interference in either instance, blaming “mistakes” in its automated content moderation systems (including AI tools that can’t tell the difference between enthusiastic follower engagement and a bot attack). Mistakes or not, with early voting in the U.S. midterms already underway, these events serve as a stark reminder that all major social media platforms need to have stronger systems in place to ensure that they serve, rather than impede, democratic communication. Access to good information can have a profound effect on political participation and speech. This is not inherently an “AI” problem: automated systems can process content at a scale that humans never could, potentially enabling better moderation at scale and alleviating the psychological load on ill-paid moderators whose jobs require them to view incredibly disturbing content. But automated systems also reproduce existing biases, struggle to understand context, and often make mistakes that disproportionately affect journalists, activists, artists, and other vulnerable and marginalized communities. And moderation errors are even more likely when the language is spoken principally by the global majority. In 2020, leaked document showed that Meta’s algorithms incorrectly deleted nonviolent Arabic-language content 77 percent of the time, while failing to detect hate speech under the company’s own policies in many instances. Where these systems are faltering in Arabic, they’re positively failing in less-resourced languages. stories.title: New Records Obtained by EFF Expose More Problems with Medicare’s AI Experiment
stories.summary: New records obtained by EFF expose additional issues with Medicare’s AI-driven prior authorization program and show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of automated decision-making . EFF sued the government back in March for information about the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model , a new Medicare program that uses AI to evaluate prior authorization requests for certain medical services. We previously released records showing that WISeR has resulted in delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Today, we’re publishing over 800 new pages of records, including: Requests for information (RFIs) or requests for corrective action plans (CAPs) sent from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to four of the six WISeR vendors, along with the vendors’ responses. Applications of 66 companies to the WISeR model, including those of the 6 selected companies. Task orders and contracts for the evaluation, implementation, and monitoring of the WISeR model. Documents obtained through EFF’s lawsuit are available here . These newly released documents show that the WISeR rollout was rushed and rocky from the start, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems. The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. The public still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples’ rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That’s because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people’s rights or deprive them of benefits they’re entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error. By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors’ access to medical care. stories.title: French Court’s Site-Blocking Orders Drive Quad9 Out Of France
stories.summary: A nonprofit service that protects internet users’ privacy is leaving France. Quad9, a free DNS resolver, has said it will reluctantly stop serving users in France on November 24. This follows a French court order that Quad9 must block access to websites that are accused of infringing the copyrights of a sports broadcaster. Forcing a responsible privacy service out of an important market is a predictable result of trying to force infrastructure providers to be copyright police. When you visit a website, a DNS resolver reads the domain name you type in—like eff.org — and translates it into a numerical IP address that’s used to direct data across the internet. A DNS resolver can see the names of websites you connect to, so its privacy policies are important. Quad9 is an NGO that’s incorporated in Switzerland, in part to protect its users from data demands. The company also helps protect users from malware and phishing by blocking domains that are known to be malicious. Services like Quad9 offer an alternative to the DNS resolvers of local internet service providers and wireless carriers, which are vulnerable to demands from law enforcement, censorship, and commercial surveillance. In a blog post explaining its decision, Quad9 explains that the French court’s order forces it to make a decision that, either way, is bad for users. It could either “extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally)” or try to identify and block users only in France—something that it can’t do reliably, and a move that could leave the company facing massive fines if it fails to block websites perfectly within France. Quad9 says it is facing about 20 other lawsuits in France seeking similar blocking orders. Rather than accept these demands, Quad9 has decided to withdraw its service from France. That is a real loss for French users who rely on the service to protect their privacy and security. It is also the right thing to do, when faced with the alternative: making promises it can’t keep, or abandoning users’ rights worldwide. Quad9’s decision will not remove any allegedly infringing material from the internet. The organization doesn’t host websites. Users looking for particular websites can easily switch to another DNS resolver. So the material targeted by copyright holders will remain online and accessible, even while they drive a privacy-protecting service out of France.…
